First, we substitute $u=2+{x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2+{x}^{3}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $3$ | $-\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{2+{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-\infty }^{3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{2+{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[{e}^{u}]_{a}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{3}-{e}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({e}^{3}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{x},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{x}=0$

- ${lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/3df1853e93a5ab2a1c1ca4114d450b29a69223bd576b059d9aef1b17c68fe5b7.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{2+{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({e}^{3}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({e}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
